qt: to the Commission Leire Pajín (S&D), Sandra Gómez López (S&D), Juan Fernando López Aguilar (S&D), Marcos Ros Sempere (S&D), Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D) Subject:

The robbery from the Villena Treasury on 27 August 2026 came at a time of growing concern over thefts of cultural property from museums in various European Member States. A recent Europol report warns of more aggressive methods targeting high-value objects. Although the Union has instruments such as Directive (EU) 2014/60 on the return of unlawfully held cultural objects, Directive (EU) 2018/1673 on combating money laundering and Directive (EU) 2024/1260 on asset recovery and confiscation, there remain shortcomings in prevention, early warning and cooperation in response to acts of theft in the Union. Does the Commission believe it necessary to review and strengthen the EU framework with a view to: 1.
establishing minimum standards for risk assessment, identification and protection of cultural property, backed by EU funding, particularly for cash-strapped local and regional museums;
setting up a permanent European early-warning system, thereby improving cooperation between national authorities, Europol and INTERPOL;

more aggressively prosecuting these offences at European level as organised crime, not least the laundering and sale of stolen cultural heritage, including on online sales platforms, thus safeguarding the common cultural heritage of all European citizens?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.11.2026) Safeguarding cultural heritage is of utmost importance to the Commission. Yet, cultural heritage protection is primarily the responsibility of Member States. EU action focuses on encouraging their cooperation and supporting their actions1. The Commission is funding a project by the International Council of Museums to fight cultural goods trafficking in Ukraine and neighbouring Member States, also covering measures to secure museums and document collections2. The European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) has a single point of contact for cultural goods trafficking. It closely cooperates with Member States, the European Union Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation (Eurojust), third countries and the International Criminal Police Organization, including through the European Multidisciplinary Platform Against Criminal Threats. Europol’s 2026 report3 about museum thefts helps museums increase preparedness. Member States shall supply Europol with information necessary for it to fulfil its objectives, including prevention of cultural goods trafficking4. It enables Europol to connect the dots between cases5. The EU action plan against trafficking in cultural goods6 encourages Member States to investigate criminal networks behind individual cases, and to implement the Nicosia Convention7. Member States are encouraged to apply Directive 2024/12608 to cultural goods trafficking committed by criminal organisations. Europol and Eurojust support law enforcement and judicial cooperation against cultural goods trafficking. In line with ProtectEU9, the Commission will propose modernised rules on organised crime in 2027. It adopted proposals to amend Europol’s and Eurojust’s mandates in 202610.
